# Research notes on Jeremiah 34

**What I could and couldn't find.** I searched with web_search and web_fetch, which ran out after a few calls. I did not reach netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org, and I found no Orthodox reading or any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace treatment of this chapter. Those headings are left out. The only Catholic material is Haydock, and on his pages for chapters 32 and 38, not 34. Most Protestant voices come from the older commentaries collected on studylight, biblehub and blueletterbible.

The Protestant disagreements here mostly don't follow denominational lines. The main debate, in vv. 4–5, splits people within the same traditions.

---

**v. 1**
- **Setting.** Guzik dates the oracle to Zedekiah's tenth or eleventh year, with the Babylonians besieging the city. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-34/
- **Earlier date.** Barnes (Presbyterian) puts the start of the siege, when the slaves were freed (vv. 8–11), early in January, in the ninth year of Zedekiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/34-18.html
- **"All the kingdoms."** Coffman says this phrase refers to Nebuchadnezzar's mixed army. It was drawn from many nations under his rule, and he could demand troops from them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/34-4.html
- **Pulpit Commentary.** It reads the phrase as "of the land", stressing how mixed the army was. It also links "all the cities" to the strongholds still holding out, such as Lachish and Azekah. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-34.html

**v. 2**
- **Who is really against Judah.** Guzik says God wanted Zedekiah to know the fall would happen by God's own will, not just Babylon's. He points to 2 Kings 25:9 to show the city really was burned. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-34/
- **Link to ch. 32.** The Pulpit Commentary thinks vv. 1–7 is probably the prophecy that got Jeremiah imprisoned, as mentioned in 32:3–5. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-34.html
- Matthew Henry places the oracle before Jeremiah's imprisonment, for the same reason. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/34-4.html

**v. 3**
- **Face to face.** Guzik notes that kings sometimes escape when a city falls, but Zedekiah would not. He would face Nebuchadnezzar, the very king who had put him on the throne and against whom he rebelled. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-34/
- **Could he still repent?** Guzik quotes Kidner wondering whether Zedekiah might still have found mercy, since God is ready to take back threats (18:8, 11). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-34/
- **The covenant he broke.** Coffman thinks Zedekiah had probably sworn loyalty to Nebuchadnezzar with the same calf-cutting ritual as v. 18. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/34-4.html

**vv. 4–5: the main point of disagreement**
- **The usual reading.** Keil & Delitzsch admit the meaning is disputed. The common view is that Zedekiah goes into exile but is not executed. He dies peacefully and is buried with royal honours. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/34-5.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed).** The promise softens the sentence, though Calvin asks whether death might not have been better after Zedekiah was blinded. To him, "die in peace" means a natural death, not a violent one. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/34-4.html
- **Conditional view.** Barnes (Presbyterian) reads the promise as conditional on surrender. Coffman (Restoration Movement) agrees, citing Dummelow and 38:17. He concludes it was never fulfilled because Zedekiah did not meet the condition. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/34-4.html
  - Barnes adds that honoured burnings imply a successful reign, the kind Zedekiah might have had as an obedient vassal to Babylon. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/34-5.htm
- **Against the conditional view.** The Pulpit Commentary calls the conditional reading a "violent interpretation". It argues that a quiet prison is "peace" compared with a cruel execution, and that exiled Jews could plausibly have mourned their king. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-34.html
  - Constable (dispensational) also thinks the promise was *probably not conditional*. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/34-4.html
- **Other readings.** Matthew Henry and Gill suggest Zedekiah might have died at peace with God, having repented in captivity. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/34-4.html and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/34-5.htm
  - Guzik notes some take the promise as conditional and unfulfilled. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-34/
- **"Burn spices."** Ellicott says spices were burned to honour dead kings. He notes the Hebrews never adopted the practice of burial by cremation. JFB adds that these honours were refused to Jehoiakim (22:18). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/34-5.htm
- **Jewish tradition.** Guzik passes on, through Clarke, a tradition that Nebuchadnezzar mocked Zedekiah in public, then allowed him an honourable burial after he died. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-34/
- **Catholic (Haydock).** Haydock (quoting Worthington) says Zedekiah was imprisoned in Babylon and buried there by the Jews, pointing to 34:5. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/jeremiah-32.html
  - On 38:17 he says even conditional prophecies are certain, and the king would have been treated differently had he complied. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/jeremiah-38.html

**v. 6**
- Guzik stresses Jeremiah's courage in delivering the message to a king who could harm him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-34/

**v. 7**
- **Why these cities.** Guzik says Nebuchadnezzar had to secure the south because of the threat from Egypt.
- **Archaeology.** He mentions the Lachish Letters, which name Lachish and Azekah. One is usually read to mean Azekah had just fallen. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-34/
- Ironside notes that only two fortified cities besides the capital were still holding out. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/jeremiah-34.html

**v. 8**
- **"Proclaim liberty."** Barnes says the wording comes from the jubilee proclamation (Leviticus 25:10). The Pulpit Commentary agrees, but notes the law actually behind the covenant is the seventh-year release. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/34-8.htm
- **Why they did it.** Ellicott suggests several motives: the siege, wanting willing freemen instead of forced labourers, and perhaps the renewed respect for the law after Josiah found it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/34-8.htm
- **Food-saving theory rejected.** Another commentator on the same page rejects Duhm's idea that the slaves were simply expelled to save food. The text implies the release benefited the slaves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/34-8.htm
- **Geneva Study Bible (Reformed).** It sees a show of holiness under danger that turned out to be hypocrisy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/34-8.htm

**v. 9**
- **What "slavery" meant.** Guzik explains four ways a Hebrew could become a slave. He argues it was usually agreed to, time-limited and heavily regulated. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-34/
- **The word "Hebrew".** Guzik quotes Thompson: Israelites normally used it of themselves only in times of servitude. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-34/
- **Debt servitude.** Constable notes Israelites sometimes became servants to pay off debts. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/34-9.html

**v. 10**
- **"They obeyed."** The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary takes this to mean reluctant obedience to the king's order, not willing respect for God's law. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/jeremiah-34.html
- Guzik thinks they were overdue slaves, not freed early. To him it was not generosity, just a stop to disobeying the law. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-34/

**v. 11**
- **Why they took the slaves back.** Guzik links it to the Babylonians pulling back to fight Egypt (37:5–10). He offers three possible motives for the first release: panic, piety or cold self-interest. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-34/
- **Spiritual application.** Guzik compares it to Satan trying to persuade believers they are not really free. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-34/
- **Clarke (Wesleyan) differs.** He thinks they promised release at the end of the seventh year, then went back on it when the time came. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-34.html
- **Superficial repentance.** The Pulpit homilies describe a repentance of fear: changed behaviour without a changed heart, which ended when the threat did. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-34.html

**vv. 12–13**
- **The Exodus link.** Calvin says God freed Israel from slavery so they would not dominate their own brothers forever. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/34-13.html
- The Pulpit Commentary: Egypt was a "house of bondmen", so Jerusalem must not become one. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-34.html

**v. 14**
- **Which year.** The Pulpit Commentary and Keil & Delitzsch both read "at the end of seven years" as meaning release in the seventh year, after six full years of service. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-34.html and https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/34-15.html
- **How long the law was ignored.** Calvin says "your fathers did not listen" should not mean the law was always ignored. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/34-13.html
  - Barnes goes further, saying the passage shows the opposite of the usual claim that these laws were neglected. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/34-9.html
  - The Treasury of Scripture Knowledge, by contrast, reckons the law was ignored for about 490 years. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/msg/jeremiah/34-14.html
- **Lutheran (Kretzmann).** The page I found is in Spanish only. It ties the release to the sabbatical year. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/34-14.html
- **Gill (Baptist).** He argues the sabbatical year cancelled debts, not servitude. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/lit/jeremiah/34-9.html

**v. 15**
- **Done in the temple.** The Pulpit Commentary places this covenant in the temple, among other solemn covenants of its kind. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-34.html
- Chuck Smith says plainly the release was right, even if late. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/34-4.html

**v. 16**
- **Contempt for God.** Bridgeway says taking the slaves back showed contempt for God and his law. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/34-4.html
- **Why it is "God's" covenant.** Calvin says the promise counted as God's covenant because it was sworn in God's presence. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/34-18.html

**v. 17**
- **Calvin.** Their proclamation counted as nothing because it was not kept. God would stop being their guardian and hand them to the sword, plague and famine. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/34-17.html
- **Clarke (Wesleyan).** God had held back the sword. Now he lets it loose, and the punishment mirrors the crime. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jeremiah-34.html
- **Matthew Henry.** "Liberty" here means being put out of God's protection. Refusing God's law means coming under his curse. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_034.cfm
- **Constable.** Masters and servants alike would end up as Nebuchadnezzar's servants. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/34-17.html
- **Pulpit Commentary.** It sees grim irony in the wording and translates "removed" as "a shuddering". https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-34.html

**v. 18**
- **The ritual.** Wesley (Methodist) explains that the calf was cut and its parts laid opposite each other in the temple. By walking between them, the people silently agreed that God could cut them apart if they broke their word. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/34-18.html
- **Old roots.** Ellicott and Calvin connect the rite to Abraham in Genesis 15. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/34-18.html
- **Gill (Baptist).** He notes some versions read "I will make the men like the calf", meaning they will be cut in pieces. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/34-18.html
- **Feinberg (quoted by Guzik).** Walking between the pieces called a curse down on oneself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-34/
- **"Cutting a covenant."** Barnes says the Hebrew phrase "to cut a covenant" comes from this rite. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/34-9.html

**v. 19**
- **No class is exempt.** Coffman says the list takes in nearly all the nation's leaders. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/34-18.html
- Calvin says it finally names the whole people. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/34-19.html
- Ironside says walking between the pieces amounted to pledging their lives. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/jeremiah-34.html

**v. 20**
- **No burial.** Constable says they would die unburied. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/34-18.html
- The Pulpit Commentary calls the line one of Jeremiah's repetitions (see 7:33). https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-34.html

**v. 21**
- **Why the king is named.** The scholar Graf took the separate mention of the king and princes to mean they had broken the covenant themselves. The Pulpit Commentary says it just singles out the most prominent people to be punished. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-34.html
- **"Gone up from you".** Barnes says this means the Babylonians had broken off the siege for now. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/34-18.html

**v. 22**
- **The return.** Guzik says Jerusalem's people thought they were saved, but God knew Babylon would come back. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-34/
- The Pulpit Commentary says v. 21's wording dates the prophecy to before the siege resumed. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-34.html

---

**A popular modern teaching (Calvary Chapel).** Chuck Smith reads the six-years-then-freedom pattern as a picture of humanity under Satan for 6,000 years, set free in Christ's millennial reign. He gives it as his own typology, not something the text says. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/34-4.html
